draft_context.source_title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
draft_context.description: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all. Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable. But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop. That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads. This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it. Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of BlueSky. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. Thanks for having me. I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think BlueSky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are. BlueSky today is really two things. There’s the BlueSky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath BlueSky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And BlueSky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol. The whole point of BlueSky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app. There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that BlueSky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of BlueSky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO? It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why BlueSky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job. I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. And so I agreed to be interim CEO initially because I was still a general partner at True and it’s a firm I helped build. It’s an amazing firm that I didn’t want to leave behind. But also, at True, we’ve had this model where we’ve moved back and forth between operator and investor. I did that while I was running Automattic. So I stepped into it. After working on it hands-on for a few months, it just got more and more fun, more and more energizing. You just feel the momentum. Also, True just switched to a new fund. So actually the timing was good where I could say, “Okay, I will switch my true role to part-time, become a venture partner,” which is what I used to be when I ran Automattic, “and I’ll go all in at BlueSky.” Tell me about the difference between being the interim CEO and the full-time CEO. When you’re the interim CEO, it feels like there are probably some boundaries in what you can do. And then the full-time CEO can obviously do everything that a full-time CEO can do. What did you feel like the boundaries were as interim CEO? On the inside, it hasn’t felt very different. I actually think the move to drop the “interim” is more important on the outside, especially for the ATmosphere and the AT Proto community, and people building on this platform and in this ecosystem just to say, “No, I’m here for the duration. This isn’t just some interim gig and then somebody else is going to show up.” So I felt like, to the outside, that makes a big difference. On the inside, the job really hasn’t changed much.. So many of my conversations here in Decoder are really about the timescale of decisions. I’ll make the comparison to my newsroom because it’s easy and it’s easy to understand. Our reporters make decisions in like 30-minute increments. A story comes up, they write it, they publish it, they move on to the next thing. I make decisions maybe in like week- or month-long increments. What are we going to cover? Where are the resources going to go? It seems like in the interim CEO role, the timescale of those decisions is necessarily short or it has the appearance of being short. And then I’m reading your note that you published when you became the full-time CEO. In the very beginning of it, you say we’re at the very beginning of the story with a decade of exciting work ahead. And I’m wondering if the timescale of the decisions you’re making now are a decade. Yeah. It touches on something really fascinating with this project. In general with decision making, one of the frameworks I really like is the reversible and irreversible decisions. A lot of decisions we make are actually reversible. I like to optimize to just make those decisions quickly and then make sure you can undo the decisions if you need to change them. And then there are a few decisions that really do have very long-term implications. They’re much harder to reverse. With this project in particular, there are decisions made at this protocol level that we’re going to have to live with for a long time. There’s a part of the company in this community that thinks very, very, very long term. This is a protocol that is going to be around for decades already. It’s in enough use that it’s going to be around for a long time. Those decisions you really need to be careful about. Then it goes all the way to things we try in the product that work or don’t work. I wasn’t in the interim mindset as much because I am also an investor in the company, so I care very much about the long-term picture. What attracts me to this whole endeavor is that it can have a really important long-term impact. I always think about, okay, how will this play out? Does this truly serve the core mission? It’s okay to make some of these harder decisions now that won’t pay off for a long time because this is going to take a while. It’s not just one company. It’s already thousands of others that are building together. That’s just a different timeframe and decision-making process than your typical just “go fast, scale as quickly as possible” [methodology]. I like it. I’m comfortable with it. I just want to stick with BlueSky, the company that is both responsible for the standard and the protocol, and the product that a lot of end users love and sometimes hate. That is the core tension of the company. The user base of BlueSky is or is not interested in the development of AT Protocol, is or is not interested in the wider ATmosphere. Under Jay’s tenure, the company was very focused on building out the protocol because the product literally could not exist unless the protocol was robust enough to stand up the product. You could see that back and forth. I have always felt that the company is far more interested in the protocol than the product, that the product was merely there to show what people could do. But now the product is big. It might be waxing or waning. It will come to whether you need to turn it into TikTok or not. Tell me where you, as a CEO with a decade-long vision for all of this, see the balance inside of BlueSky between the product, the thing that looks like a Twitter app, and the protocol, the thing that should enable thousands upon thousands of other social experiences? I see the BlueSky app and the product as enabling the ATmosphere. It’s an on-ramp, or maybe a lobby to the ATmosphere where it’s just a great way to get lots of people in, get people exposed to the idea, and then realize as you use the product, “Oh, there are other things here. This isn’t just a microblogging app.” An example from the last couple of months that’s gone super well is this format called Standard Site that emerged. The history of that is that BlueSky’s a microblogging app. People are asking for longer-form posting. A bunch of other apps started popping up that were for newsletters and blogging. In particular, three apps called Leaflet, Pocket, and Off Print. They got together and said, “Hey, why don’t we define a format for all of us to work together on the ATmosphere for all of the posts that we publish?” We looked at it and said, “Great, we can now take that and surface it in our app.” So now, if you’re posting a blog post on Leaflet, it just shows up in the BlueSky app and we can make that a seamless experience. This went over really well to the point where now WordPress is supporting Standard Site and lots of other publishing platforms. They’re realizing the benefit of, “If I just publish to this new format now, it’s going to show up and work across all these other platforms without me having to do anything.” It’s caused this really nice ripple effect throughout the ecosystem where people can work together just by using this format. Nobody has to do deals with each other. Nobody has to get permissions and no money has to change hands. And it’s just taken off. I’m hoping more and more BlueSky users will see those kinds of integrations and go, “Oh, cool. I’m not just getting BlueSky content here. I’m getting content from all these other apps, all these other networks. And it just works. I don’t have to do anything. I don’t have to go sign up for 10 different apps. It’s just one signup, one account, and it just works.” You’re describing two different kinds of things. There’s a lot of work to be done at the protocol level. There’s a lot of work to be done to support new kinds of experiences like Standard Site. Then there’s BlueSky, a product which has 45 million people, and probably needs to be substantially bigger if it wants to be the aggregator for a massive network that can displace some of the other social products out there. That needs to be a lot of things to a lot of people. It needs to find different kinds of product market fit. How big is BlueSky the company now, and how is it structured to point in two different directions? We’re now at 50 people, still very small. The biggest challenge is clearly trying to do everything you’ve described with a small team. We do have an ecosystem of hundreds and thousands of others working on it, so that helps. We do our best to coordinate everyone. I would say we’re making good progress. We’re seeing good momentum, especially on the ATmosphere side. The things we look at are the number of daily active apps on the network, which has doubled since the beginning of the year. It’s about to hit a thousand. We look at SDK downloads for our tools that have tripled. It’s going to hit a million downloads a month by later this year. Those are the numbers that show that not only is it scaling, but we’re able to scale it with the team that we have. How is that team structured? About 50 people, all remote, structured into small teams. I’m a big believer that six to eight person teams, highly aligned, highly incentivized, and motivated are the way to get things done. Probably the only way to get things done. There are three core product teams. There’s the app team that deals with the BlueSky app. There’s the ATmosphere team that does all the developer-facing stuff. And then there’s a third product team called the exploration team, and that’s a new team that Jay has stood up and is running. We actually just launched a new version of the product they’re working on, Attie. Think of it as AI layered on top of the ATmosphere and what you can do with that. Those are our three core product teams, and they’re each customer-facing. Consumer-facing, developer-facing, and then we’ll find out from the AI product what the market fit is there. We have a bunch of support teams that support those three core teams and that are pretty typical. We’ve got a legal team, et cetera, et cetera. I would say it’s a team that’s a very low ego, high agency. That is kind of the ethos. Low drama, just a lot of get-shit-done energy. Really collaborative. Whenever I think about new social products and how they might scale, especially with explosive user growth – up until recently, the conventional wisdom is you’ve got to scale trust and safety and moderation linearly with the size of your user base. Maybe we’re going to add AI to this and that linear relationship will break, or maybe it’ll actually get even more costly because token spend will get more costly than having human moderators, or there’ll be more false positives and we’re going to be even angrier. So you have to have more humans in the loop. It’s really unclear to me how that’s going to work. You’ve obviously been scaling BlueSky as a consumer social product. Then you have the complexity of, “We’re hooking onto lots and lots of other products that are putting content in front of people.” How does the moderation layer work? And have you seen it be a linear increase in cost with the size of the network and the user base? Moderation is huge in any social product. In addition to our 50-person team, we do have contractors that help us with moderation. What we’ve done differently is that our whole moderation system is composable or pluggable. It’s not just us that can label content and moderate it. Anybody can do it and add labels. It’s part of the protocol. Anybody else who builds products can decide if they want to use those labels or not. So if somebody on our moderation team labels something as, let’s say, AI slop, everybody else who’s building in this ecosystem can take advantage of that piece of data. They don’t have to, but they can. So what we’re seeing and what we’ve seen is we have our moderation team, but then there are other teams that have decided to moderate label content the way they want. For example, maybe the first non-BlueSky project on the protocol was BlackSky. And it’s now become a thriving company on its own. It’s a team building all kinds of interesting things. And they started out by saying, “Hey, we want to build a version of this network that is optimized for Black users and their needs. And we want to have our own moderation policies.” And they are able to do that and plug that in. But everything they’re doing is still part of the larger network. And now there are hundreds and thousands of these kinds of systems. This has really helped where the moderation burden isn’t all on one team that has to scale and look at everything. There should be lots of different teams and lots of different systems because each network, each community has its own idea of what moderation should look like. So we feel like this kind of distributed moderation approach is more powerful. That said, yes, we’re continuing to scale up ours, but it’s manageable. It’s a lot of work, but it’s manageable. It’s worth it when the whole network can benefit from it. The next part of that story that’s going to be really interesting is that the biggest thing we’re actually working on with AT Proto, the next evolution of the protocol, is private data. We all know that the public square, public social networking has reached a certain scale. And there are a lot of people who want to retreat into more private spaces. We’ve seen explosive growth in group chats. We’re all in a million group chats. This has been the number-one request from our community, from our developers: “Let us build more private, membership-based, various versions of private spaces on this protocol.” We’re in the middle of building that. It’s a community effort. It’s rolling out very soon. Now, moderation moves and gets broken up into even more and smaller spaces. People can decide, “If I don’t like a network or I don’t like the way it’s moderated, [I can] go start my own.” Go start your own community. That’s the most interesting thing ahead of us, because right now everything on AT Proto is public. It can only be used for a completely public product. Once we enable private data, I think that it’s like 10 or 100X the number of use cases we can serve. Not to be reductive, but I think it’s useful to talk about this in comparison to other social products people might be more familiar with. With AT Protocol right now and the ATmosphere, everything is very public. The models in my head are Twitter, and RSS, and massive broad-based publishing platforms, right? One-to-many. I think what you’re describing is much more like a Reddit style approach, where you have smaller, closed communities. Some of them can be totally private unless you’re invited in. And yet, they’re still on the ATmosphere in some way. Is that right? That’s right. The trade-off has traditionally been that if you want to be on a launch network, you have to be on a public network. Or if you want to control, have ownership over your own community, you have to set up your own thing. You have to run your own server or you have to run your own forum. There’s clearly a need for that because there are lots of those out there. But the challenge is each one of those is now a little island. And you have to convince people. We think we can pull off as the best of both worlds. When you build a community or private space on AT Proto, it’s absolutely 100% owned by you. It’s not owned by BlueSky or by any company. It’s just like everything else on a protocol. It’s owned by the users, not by the platform. So it’s really truly yours. You can move it around. You can make all the decisions. But because it’s on a shared protocol, all of these communities plug together. You can go to a place like BlueSky and get all your notifications in one place. You can see what’s going on across everything. You just need one login, one place to check, but you still have the independence and the identity of these individual communities. That is something that no other platform can do right now. You’re either on the large platform owned and controlled place, or you run your own and you’re a little siloed. We think we can solve that. We see the energy behind this idea and the number of things people are already prototyping is very palpable. I have to ask you the other Decoder question because I’m very curious where this idea came from and how you decided to bet on it. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for making decisions? I already talked a little bit earlier about the reversible and irreversible decisions. The hardest thing about running any project is that, especially if it’s successful, it’s just an endless flow of things you have to prioritize and decide on. I find you could make that a lot less daunting and exhausting if you move a lot of decisions into this category of “they’re not that big a deal.” Let’s make it easy to experiment and reverse things, and really only focus on the truly long-term impactful things that we have to get right. You have this lightness or almost playfulness about some of these things, where it’s just not that big a deal. Let’s just try something. Let’s be creative and improvisational about it. This is a lot of how Automattic runs. I actually credit a lot of that to Matt Mullenweg’s approach to first running an open-source project. Inside Automattic, there are a lot of jazz analogies because Matt started out as a jazz musician. Just this improvisational, “don’t take it so seriously if you don’t have to.” There are very serious decisions we have to make as well. For those, I like spending a lot of one-on-one time with the leaders, and then gathering and going through the list and talking through the trade-offs. Making sure that at least in a good cadence, monthly or maybe quarterly, we go through and make those hard trade-off decisions and don’t leave the room until we say, “No, we’re only doing these two things on the important list. We can’t do everything. Let’s voice all the ideas, but get to agreement on the few things we’re trying to get done. They can talk to each other when you want, but that’s not the main use of it. There are a lot of people who run ActivityPub instances who don’t even want to talk to other Mastodon servers. They just want to run their own thing. They don’t want to talk to AT Proto, but they can if they want. I don’t know what a good example is from other platforms. But they’re both going to be around for a long time and they’re just slightly different tools. They’re both in the social space, but they’re different tools that you reach to for different types of use cases. I’ll put it this way: In my mind, both can be wildly successful, and it’s not one or the other. AT Proto doesn’t need to eat ActivityPub to be successful, or vice versa. We’ve already seen that. I want to end by talking about the consumer app a little bit more. We’ve talked a lot about the protocol, the ATmosphere, the standards. We’ve gotten all the way to the internet engineering task force in this conversation. We’ve been in the weeds of how the technology works and how it’s governed. And right next to that is, well, it’s an election year here in the United States. And a lot of people truly believe that BlueSky is the wild progressive social media network and it is a bubble of one kind. X is a very different kind of bubble. It’s the hard-right network that has vastly more AI-generated anime porn on it. There’s not some thing that is actually the global town square. That thing has maybe gone away and all the social networks have fragmented. Do you want BlueSky to have the reputation it has? Do you want it to get bigger? Do you think that the right answer is someone starts a MAGA BlueSky and it interoperates the way that it needs to? This is the perception of the consumer product. Do you want that to change, and how would you change it? Yes, we definitely want that to change. It is already changing. It certainly wasn’t designed to attract one specific group of people. It works for anyone. What we see is there is a lot of political discourse on BlueSky and any of these open networks. People are very engaged. What we’ve seen in the lead up to the election so far – we’ve hosted a lot of live election feeds, and we see a lot of really good feedback from our users, a lot of engagement, a lot of, “This is actually really interesting content about this topic.” Whereas on other platforms, I think these election topics just get completely overwhelmed by slop and spam. It’s just noise and chaos. What we’re focusing on is to deliver a live experience. We do it around elections. We do it around sports as well, very successfully, where the people on the network that participate get a really good experience and get really good content. Once we have that, then hopefully we can just keep expanding to more and more types of users and use cases. We’re an open network for anyone and we don’t want to serve just one type of user base. I’ve seen it already in the last few months, really trend in the right direction where we just have more and more people show up and build their own corners of the network. It sort of balances out over time. We don’t just have a few topics you’re super deep on, but it just gets more and more diverse. In my opinion, yes, it’s a public square, but we don’t need everybody talking at the same time. Policy is very loaded, but if you’re super into sports, you’re not going to be into all sports. I’m super into the San Francisco Giants, so that’s what I want to follow. I don’t need to follow all of sports, and that’s fine. It can be like that with all topics. It just needs to be civil and positive and we need to have the tools that if it goes off the rails, people can regulate it and can have a good experience instead of it just devolving into a shouting match. By “people can regulate it,” you mean people can moderate their own feeds, not regulators can moderate speech? 100%, yes. Just checking. That’s important. Build their own feeds, pick their own feeds. We have very good tools for people to mute and block. We spend a lot of energy on making sure it stays positive because again, we’re interested in social media that actually serves the common or the public good. That’s not going to work if it’s just people yelling. You’ve talked a lot about the network. Even in this answer, I said BlueSky the app has this reputation, and you started talking about the network. It’s true, the network can serve everybody. Anybody can start whatever kind of app on the ATmosphere they want and they can go target the users they want. But I want to push you again on BlueSky the app. The thing that has a brand that exists out in the world that is totally divorced from the technical specifications of the ATmosphere. There is BlueSky the app and it does have a reputation. Do you want more users from X to leave X and join BlueSky and expand what that brand is for people? Yes. It can stay on X too. You don’t have to pick one or the other, but yes. Have you talked to Elon about federating X? I suspect he’s not interested. No, same answer with Threads. It would be full circle, right? BlueSky started inside Twitter, and then Twitter went away and became X. And then if X adopted AT Proto, then the whole original idea of the project would actually come to fruition. Yeah. This is Jack Dorsey saying Twitter wants to be AT Protocol, not a product. Here we are, and that’s BlueSky in big ways, but it is also a product. People know what that logo means. Political pundits say “the BlueSky crowd,” and that signifies whatever they want it to signify. I’m just wondering if you want to break that branding in any meaningful way. Yeah, we want to expand it. “Breaking” is maybe the wrong word, but yes, we want to expand more and more so that BlueSky means not just one thing, not just liberal politics, for example. I will point to sports as an example from the last year. We’ve made a very concerted effort to bring on sports leagues and sports writers, and it’s worked really well. There are a ton of sports conversations now on the app, and those people come here for the sports, not for the liberal politics. It’s possible to expand. In politics, it’s probably our hardest challenge because we have one type of user base there that’s very active. That’s good too. They are super active, and they’re very much at the forefront of politics and very engaged and very informed. But we can just keep adding more communities so that it balances out. It feels like we’re going to have to have you back, particularly as these private communities launch, to talk about where things go from here. But this has been great. Thank you so much for being on Decoder . Thank you very much for having me. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email! ]]>
paragraphs: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder , because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all.

Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable.

But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team.

Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop.

That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads.

draft_context.source_title: Creality Falcon T1 review: A 5-star 5-in-1 laser engraver for businesses
draft_context.description: The idea behind the Falcon T1 is inspired but not unique: essentially, one machine that can replace five, with swappable modules that enable it to engrave and cut wood, mark metal, and engrave crystal, all via a set of interchangeable laser modules sold separately. Swap the module, and the machine becomes a different tool, much like many other workshop tools, so from that point of view the concept is far from unique. This means that if you’re a business short on space, or even if it’s not, then a machine like this will be appealing. There are, of course, a few catches: the first is that the machine ships with one module, the 20W fibre laser, which I’m looking at in this review. However, the key to this machine is that it’s a 5-in-1, so as a first look I’ll be using this module and then covering the others later. It's worth noting that each of those additional modules costs anything from £859 upwards, so the more you buy, the more cost effective this machine becomes, when compared with dedicated machines. (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) There is another slight issue, which Creality has addressed to a point: this machine is designed for small products. In this review, the fibre laser is used on a small metal object, which is fine with the fibre laser and the 175 x 175mm work area. However, as you switch to the diode modules, you may want a larger workspace, which is where the additional lenses and the conveyor for batch production come into play. In this first-look review, I have based my use and findings on the 20W Fibre Laser module, and I’ll update with the additional modules when they arrive. Creality Falcon T1: Price & availability The Falcon T1 is listed on the official Creality website for $2249 , and on the UK site for £1999 . That buys the machine with the 20W Fibre Laser module. Additional modules start from $809 / £859 each, so a full five-laser system quickly escalates the price. Accessories add more again: the Rotary Kit Pro, a conveyor, smoke purifier, flexible fixture, knife bed, and UV riser all available separately, creating a comprehensive ecosystem for businesses. Creality Falcon T1: Design Specs Modules : 20W diode, 40W diode, 20W fibre, 60W MOPA, 5W UV (sold separately) Wavelengths : 445nm diode, 1064nm fibre and MOPA, 355nm UV Working area : 175 x 175mm (UV internal engraving 70 x 70mm) Spot size : 0.12 x 0.14mm (20W diode), 0.05mm (fibre/MOPA), 0.014mm (UV) Processing accuracy : 0.01mm or better; positioning accuracy +/-0.01mm Maximum speed : 10,000mm/s Cutting : 8mm basswood (20W diode), 12mm basswood (40W diode), 0.2mm anodised aluminium (fibre) Camera : HD positioning, autofocus and monitoring Display : 4.3in detachable touchscreen; USB, cloud and app control Software : Falcon Design Space, LightBurn, GRBL; Windows and macOS Safety : Class 1 enclosed, lid-open stop, emergency stop, key lock, temperature, smoke and flame detection Dimensions : 464 x 312 x 509mm Getting started with the T1 is a relatively quick process once the machine is unboxed. The machine is almost fully assembled, with only the build plate, screen, power, and module needing to be fitted. Most of the few parts that need attention before you start just need to be plugged in, with the large laser module essentially slotting into the back of the machine. To access the slot, you need to rotate the machine's body. The T1 itself weighs in at 20 kg. I couldn’t find official figures, so this is the result from me putting the machine on the scales. The 20W module weighs 3.2kg, and you do need to leave yourself a little room for manoeuvre to access the module slot. The module is a box of electronics with the laser lens, and each module is essentially of the same design, just utilising different technology for the beam. As this is a space-saving exercise, the module measures in at 22 x 95 x 175mm. The installation process to a working state takes a couple of minutes, with the actual tool swap, which is usually the time-consuming part, taking no more than a suggested 15 seconds. To swap modules, you first need to switch on the machine. This should raise the centre section. If not, when the screen has finished the boot sequence, tap the tool change button; you’ll need to do this if you’ve been working with one of the modules and need to swap. Then switch the machine off; there’s no hot swapping. Push the lock button on top, withdraw the installed module, then insert the next module, rotate the machine back into position, and power on. This is the simplest tool change I think I’ve come across for any machine, and while it may not take 15 seconds for the entire process, that takes closer to two minutes, I managed 5 seconds for the actual module change; it’s that simple. Once everything is set up and in position, the T1, as a machine, is relatively tall and fully enclosed with a large tinted viewing panel, measuring 464 x 312 x 509mm. Compared with similar machines, the footprint is pretty standard, as is the height. The height, however, increases as the entire protective cover rises when you load and unload materials, and again when you change modules. On the side of the machine is the detachable 4.3-inch touchscreen, which I liked more than I expected. It uses a magnet to attach to the right-hand side on an extendable cable, so it stores away neatly out of the way and pulls round to the front when you want it. The screen itself is extremely responsive and gives access to most of what you need without a computer, though the excellent desktop software gives you full control. Before using the machine, the inserted module needs to be calibrated. The box includes a calibration chart and a few other items of material that can be used to do this. The process is relatively straightforward, and Creality has created several tutorial videos to guide you through the process. As the lid is lifted, you can place it on the removable work bed, which offers height, and the design enables various positioning options, especially for awkward objects. With the setup that I was sent, I was only able to work with metal due to the fibre module, and as I went through the test materials, there was almost nothing to clean up afterwards. From experience, I know that using a diode head generates far more dust and particles that need to be cleaned away. It’s also worth noting that the exhaust fan and dust guard both detach for cleaning. I’ll also note that no air purifier was supplied with my machine, so I connected an existing filter from another manufacturer using a little ducting, and it worked perfectly, although with full manual control. If you already own a purifier, that is worth knowing; you will lose the integrated feedback and control, but you’ll save some cash. (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) Creality Falcon T1: Features The module swap is the headline feature here, and although I only had a single module to work with, it seemed easy enough. However, swapping heads and recalibration are features that would set this apart from competitors. I was unable to check this, so it could be as simple as a quick swap or require far more time; again, I’ll update when further modules arrive. An area that I am interested in seeing work is the calibration handling; it looks to be the clever part. Once you have calibrated each module with the supplied cards, swapping between modules doesn’t require recalibration, allowing you to move quickly between materials and processes. If, however, you do move the machine around the workshop, as I did, a quick recalibration is sensible before starting again. Compared with the usual business of changing laser heads, the whole process seems quick. (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) Inside the machine is an HD camera that works through the desktop software and enables you to place designs onto material accurately; this is essential when you are engraving something where you only get one go, such as a phone, lens or laptop. Everything is calibrated so positioning is precise rather than approximate, and the software will map designs onto curved surfaces such as bottles. The AI tools are more useful than they sound and far better than the usual gimmicky template images you see. Instead, they can be used to generate relief images to create coins from images sourced from Salisbury Museum, engraving them into blank metal coins, and it worked remarkably well. There is also automatic layout, batch filling, and colour-engraving assistance for metals, and the multicolour engraving produced by the fibre module through the software is impressive. Creality Falcon T1: Performance Setup took around 10 minutes, as the machine arrived pre-assembled and factory-calibrated. I just needed to attach the cables and install the 20W fibre module before running through the calibration process, following the online videos, and then started with the test files from the supplied USB stick. Later, when connected to a MacBook Pro, the Falcon Design Space was equally easy to use, and from there I could lay out my own designs, access the live camera feed, and position artwork precisely over the material, eliminating the guesswork. The software really deserves a big mention, and I’ve used it before on previous Falcon machines. It’s just well thought out and lets you get straight to work rather than faffing around with settings. Unlike fibre lasers that hand you off to third-party software, this is fully integrated with the hardware, and that integration pays off constantly in workflow. Everything worked seamlessly and felt stable from the outset, one of the issues I often find with fibre lasers intended for the professional market. Being able to set a job running from another room or to position a design against a live camera feed, rather than by guesswork, turns what is often a fiddly process into something straightforward. At the time of review, I’m only testing the one module, but will update on the ease of swapping and the software's recognition of each new option once installed. Using the Fibre laser gave me quite a bit of flexibility with materials, including engraving on metal. It was incredibly fast and accurate, with fine, crisp edges and detail. Most designs engraved onto various types of metal were completed in a few seconds, with most complex designs completed within 30 seconds. This is also one of the first machines that makes working in colour with metal engraving relatively easy, and it is a prime example of where AI comes into play. Essentially, load the image, and the AI converts it into what is needed. Although the hit rate on this isn’t 100%, it does make things easier than almost all other solutions I’ve tried, with only the XTool option being on a par. You can then go in and adjust the colours, as needed. As ever, a little experimentation is needed, but it’s just about as smooth a process as I’ve yet come across in this type of work. On average, these designs, at the maximum size I tried (160 x 160), took around an hour. There were a few glitches along the way, but I was pleased to see that the software lets you generate test charts to test the material before you start. Using the module with metals and the engraving quality with the 20W fibre module is exceptional. Speed and resolution are among the best I have seen, on a par with the strongest dedicated fibre machines, although the weaker power does mean more passes when embossing. To test this, I had a high-resolution image from Salisbury Museum of a coin, and once it was processed through the software, it was embossed onto one of the coin blanks. The effect of this coin, due to its age and relief, was subtle, but when a few other designs were transformed, and the results were pronounced. This is an amazing process, although, whereas the other uses are relatively quick, the process of creating an embossed coin took 13 hours, so roughly 26 hours for the two sides if you want to go down that route. A 40W or the MOPA will make a big difference to this speed and will be one of the most exciting aspects of this engraver. (Image credit: Alastair Jennings) With that modular design, the 20w will hopefully see an upgrade in the future. One thing worth knowing is that, with this machine, and for that matter, higher-quality fibre material is important: cheap metal items engrave, but they do not look great afterwards. In contrast, a quality stainless steel piece under the same laser looks superb. If you are producing items to sell, buy decent blanks. The 175 x 175mm working area proved decent enough for the small metal objects, which is exactly what the fibre machines tend to suit: keyrings, coins, tags, and similar personalised items. For anything larger, it will feel restrictive. Through the review, I also tested the conveyor, one of the few accessories supplied, and setting it up requires considerably more room; it also requires you to disengage the lid's safety feature, so protective glasses are required. I was surprised to see that none have been provided. However, again, this is quite common for this level of machine, and the results and speed increase for batch production are impressive. What really stands out is how it can automatically recognise the objects placed on the surface and engrave without you needing to align each individually. If you do a lot of batch work, the conveyor makes sense, and again it shows the potential for the machine, which I only feel like through the review I am touching on. Creality Falcon T1: Final verdict In this test, I gave the 20 fibre module a good run, and it instantly gives a good idea of its potential, once those other modules are purchased. Add in the 20W and 40W diode modules, which handle wood and acrylic cutting; the 60W MOPA, which most professionals will be interested in for deep and colored metal work; and the 5W UV module for glass, ceramics and internal crystal engraving, this machine really makes sense. Couple all that with the rotary kit and the smoke purifier, and you have a professional eco-system that starts to look extremely appealing. If you regularly work with wood, leather, metal, and glass, the modular concept makes sense, and buying the modules you need rather than five separate machines will save both money and a great deal of space in the long run. On reviewing the fibre module, the engineering and software quality do show potential, but if you’re only going to be using one module then this is an expensive option. However, add in at least one or two additional modules and it makes sense in both cost and size. You work across several materials. If you regularly customise wood, acrylic, metal, glass, and crystal, a single enclosure with interchangeable modules can replace several machines and save considerable workshop space. You produce small batches commercially. Fast repeated engraving, camera-assisted positioning and the optional conveyor suit personalised products and regular commercial orders on small items. draft_context.source_title: Backpacks, USB hubs, and more: the essential accessories every student needs for their Mac
draft_context.description: Back to school season is here, with students preparing to head to school and college up and down the land. If that’s you and you’ve got one of the best Macs ready to take with you, you might be thinking about kitting it out with some handy accessories. While Apple’s Macs are brilliant devices, they can often be taken to another level with the help of some choice add-ons. Here, we’ve put together some of the best Mac accessories for heading back to school, from protective bags to keep your Mac safe to useful extras that bring new features and comfort to your Mac experience. Each one is a worthy addition to your setup. And don’t forget, if you’re getting accessories from Apple itself, be sure to look on Apple’s education store for special student discounts. Many third-party retailers also run back-to-school sales, and these often cover more than just Apple products, so don’t forget to shop around before you pull the trigger. Laptop backpack: Timbuk2 Authority Backpack (Image credit: Timbuk2) With all the traveling to and from lectures — not to mention flights if you’re studying far from home — student life can take its toll on your Mac. That’s why it’s important to keep it protected to ensure it lasts as long as possible. A great option is the Timbuk2 Authority Backpack, which is our pick for the best laptop backpack money can buy. It can hold a MacBook of any size, so whether you get a MacBook Air or a MacBook Pro , you know it’ll be safely stowed inside. It’s also got a dedicated iPad pocket and tons of extra storage for all the accessories you might need to carry. There’s plenty of padding to protect against damage, and it’s also extremely comfortable to wear, even when loaded up with all your kit. And with special protection against downpours and showers, it’ll keep its contents dry and safe come rain or shine. Portable power bank: Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K) (Image credit: TechRadar) Arrived at a lecture only to find your Mac is about to run out of power? Ensure that never happens again with the Anker 737 Power Bank (PowerCore 24K) . This portable battery will keep your laptop juiced up and has enough charge for several other devices to boot. With a massive 140W of output, it’s got enough power to charge up a MacBook Pro and an iPhone and still have extra left over. With three ports, you can hook up several devices at once, and the built-in display tells you the power bank’s battery health, output level from each port, and how much charge it’s got left. It’s also safe to take on planes, which is good for students traveling home, and its cuboid shape makes it surprisingly easy to pack into tight corners. It’s capable, well designed, and could be just what you need when your battery is running low. USB-C hub: Satechi OntheGo 7-in-1 Multiport Adapter (Image credit: Satechi) While the MacBook Pro comes with HDMI and an SDXC slot alongside USB-C ports, it’s one of the few Macs to offer anything more than USB-C. If you’ve got a range of incompatible accessories, you’ll want a hub to put things right. The Satechi OntheGo 7-in-1 Multiport Adapter is a USB-C hub that can do exactly that. It plugs into a USB-C port on your Mac and offers a range of extra connectivity, including two USB-A slots, a USB-C port that can deliver up to 80W of Power Delivery juice to your devices, an SD card reader, a microSD reader, HDMI 2.0 and Gigabit Ethernet. But it’s about much more than its connectivity. This device’s clever design and extendable cable make it incredibly portable, while its included magnet allows you to quickly snap it to a surface without the risk of losing it. It’s an ingenious product that solves a problem and looks good while doing so. Monitor: BenQ PD2706QN (Image credit: Collin Probst // Future ) As a student, chances are you’ll be spending a lot of time working on your Mac. But if that means hunching over a MacBook for hours on end, you’ll quickly feel the strain. Take it from me — I used to work exclusively on a laptop, but suffered terrible back pain until I bought myself an external monitor that vastly improved my ergonomic situation. Our pick here is the BenQ PD2706QN. Not only will it help create a more comfortable work situation, but it boasts excellent features that are worth having in their own right. That includes an expansive 27-inch display size with a 1440p resolution and 100Hz refresh rate, which combine to make on-screen content sharp and scrolling smooth. It offers excellent color accuracy, hitting 95% of the P3 color space, and with 90 watts of Power Delivery, it’s got enough output to keep any MacBook powered up directly from the monitor itself. We also love its Nano Matte coating option that vanquishes reflections in a pinch. For a more affordable option, there’s the BenQ GW2486TC , which is one of our favorite MacBook Pro monitors . Its 23.8-inch frame and 1080p resolution are a little lower than the PD2706QN, but it’s a well-built display with excellent ergonomic customization that won’t break the bank. That makes it one of the best monitors on the market. Obviously, an external display isn’t particularly practical for going to lectures, but if you spend a lot of time working in your dorm, it can be a lifesaver. Laptop stand: Lamicall Laptop Stand (Image credit: Future) If you don’t want an external monitor but are still in search of something to boost your ergonomics, consider a laptop stand . These raise your MacBook to a more comfortable height without the expensive of an additional screen. Our choice here is the Lamicall Laptop Stand, which is sized to fit any MacBook available. The key thing with any laptop stand is you need it to not only raise your device, but to do so safely, and that’s exactly what you get here. Lamicall’s product features a solid base to prevent it from tipping over and rubber pads that firmly keep your laptop in place. Yet at 3.25lbs (1.47kg), it’s light enough to carry with you, and it folds down to easily fit into a backpack. It also comes fully assembled, negating the need to put it together when it arrives. Those factors all make it an ideal option for students. Mouse and keyboard: Logitech MX Master 4 and Gamakay TK75 V2 (Image credit: Future) An external mouse and keyboard are a must if you raise your Mac up to a new height, as you won’t be able to use your Mac’s built-in keyboard in its new position. But they also come in handy even if you don’t use a stand by bringing extra features and comfort to your setup. If you’re looking for a mouse, your best choice by far is the Logitech MX Master 4 , the latest entry in the incredibly popular MX Master range. Its ergonomic shape is complemented by a handy thumb scroll wheel and a gesture button that lets you move the mouse to activate native macOS gestures. Its main scroll wheel can also automatically switch between ratcheting through individual notches and spinning freely. As for a keyboard, you can’t go wrong with the Gamakay TK75 V2 , which is one of the best keyboards you can buy. Its mechanical switches are supremely comfy and surprisingly quiet, meaning you won’t disturb anyone around you, and it looks great too with its attractive design. The price is affordable and it’s compact enough to lug across campus without a worry. Bonus: AppleCare+ (Image credit: Apple) With all that traveling to and from lectures, you might be concerned about bumps and bruises — or worse — heading the Mac’s way. If you’re concerned, Apple’s AppleCare+ program covers the company’s devices and can provide some peace of mind. It’s not a physical accessory, but it can be a worthwhile addon for your Mac. AppleCare+ allows for unlimited accident repairs, including drops and liquid spills, plus 24/7 priority support from Apple. All repairs are done with genuine Apple parts so you know you’re getting quality. The price you pay for AppleCare+ depends on the Mac you get — for instance, coverage for a MacBook Pro costs $10.49 a month or $104.99 a year. Apple also offers AppleCare+ with Theft and Loss as an optional extra. Here, you get coverage if your device is lost or stolen, and you can make up to two claims every 12 months. Note that this only covers iPhones, iPads and Apple Watches — not Macs — so it’s mainly useful if you have these devices rather than as coverage for your Mac or Mac accessories. Finally, there’s also AppleCare One . This covers up to three products (including ones you already own) and includes theft and loss coverage for iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch with up to three claims every 12 months. It costs $19.99 a month. Additional products can be added at any time for $5.99 a month each. ]]>
